title: Glory in the Flesh
speaker: Josh Wyatt
card_summary: Josh joins John 1:1 and 1:14: the Word was God, and the Word became flesh. The glory that kept Israel at a distance now tabernacles among humanity in Jesus, the true sanctuary and high priest. At the cross holy judgment falls on Christ so sinners receive grace without truth being softened.

movements.heading: Doctrine is not a substitute for inspiration
bullets: Backhanded compliments—from “smarter than you look” to “your sermon didn’t feel long”—establish that words carry weight. Josh says no words matter more than John 1:1-18.
He answers the objection that doctrine is less useful than inspiration: the incarnation is the church’s hope and carries eternal consequences. John wrote so people would know whom to trust.
The pulpit must offer Christ rather than warm uplift. Listeners should not grade the sermon but examine themselves: the soul does not need soup; it needs a Savior.

movements.heading: The Word became flesh: the Bible’s center
bullets: John 1:1 and 1:14 hold together the incarnation: the Word was God, and the Word became flesh. The infinite becomes finite, eternity enters time, and the Creator enters creation.
Josh reads John 1:14-18: witnesses see the Son’s glory; he is full of grace and truth; grace comes through him; and he makes the unseen God known.

A Star Wars viewing-order illustration calls incarnation the Bible’s “missing movie.” Greeks held too low a view of deity; Jews thought God too exalted to take flesh. John answers both: God truly came near so his glory could be seen.

movements.heading: God tabernacled among his people
bullets: Josh reads John through the Bible’s dwelling theme. Eden held fellowship with God, sin destroyed peace, and God chose to close the distance himself.
The wilderness tabernacle stood among Israel’s tents, its ordinary exterior concealing glory. Cloud and fire sheltered, illuminated, and guided the camp as God walked among his people.
God is not confined to one nation or mountain. Romans includes Jew and Gentile; Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that true worshipers worship in Spirit and truth.
Hebrews identifies the earthly sanctuary as a shadow of the heavenly reality fulfilled in Christ. Jesus is high priest, mediator, and the true tabernacle who enters once for all by his own blood.
The Word camped among his people. The incarnation is why the church sings, gathers, and proclaims the gospel; Wesley’s hymn answers with incarnate deity and Emmanuel.

movements.heading: Holy glory is dangerous apart from Christ
bullets: Ancient reluctance arose from a high view of holiness, while modern presumption often comes from a high view of self. God’s presence is not a warm accessory for unrepentant sinners.
Sinai burns, smokes, and trembles. Like a father carefully holding a newborn, God sets boundaries because people cannot bear his unveiled power.
Moses asks to see God’s glory but cannot see his face and live. The proper response is humility, confession, and flight to Jesus—not treating God as subordinate.
John’s claim is astonishing precisely because glory fatal to mere humans has now been seen in the incarnate Son.

movements.heading: Believers receive more access than Israel had
bullets: Exodus says even Moses could not enter the glory-filled tent, yet John says believers have seen God’s glory. Attempts to silence that witness only spread it: Stephen dies and a Pharisee becomes a missionary.
Israel viewed the sanctuary from outside; believers have Emmanuel with them, the Spirit within them, and peace through Jesus’ blood. All believers are a royal priesthood beholding glory in Christ.
Josh sees present glory in Christians pursuing holiness as foreigners and strangers. The Son makes God known through transformed hearts, endurance, truth, holiness, and his enduring word.

movements.heading: Fire illustrates glory and the cross
bullets: A family fire recalls Exodus: divine glory is bright, captivating, and dangerous. Fire teaches reverence, exposes flaws, and refines before it comforts.
Malachi’s refiner and John’s grace and truth meet in images that burn without consuming God’s people—the bush and guiding pillar.
At Calvary, consuming judgment falls on Jesus so the benefits of glory fall on God’s children. Josh prays that sons and daughters will be drawn to God like his son is drawn to flame.

movements.heading: Jesus is full of grace and truth
bullets: Grace and truth can be distinguished but not separated in Christ. Human beings alternate between affectionate compromise and harsh honesty; Jesus holds both in perfect fullness.
He never softens truth to appear gracious and never withholds grace to state truth. His welcome of Zacchaeus and the hostility of religious leaders prepare the extended example in John 8.

movements.heading: The adulterous woman: grace satisfies truth
bullets: Religious leaders publicly present a guilty woman and invoke Moses to trap Jesus. The absent man exposes selective use of the law and contempt for both justice and the woman.

Josh compares the scene with Solomon’s public judgment, then identifies Jesus as the wisdom of God. His call for the sinless person to cast first exposes the accusers; his refusal to condemn anticipates bearing the woman’s debt.
“Neither do I condemn you” is grace; “leave your life of sin” is truth. Jesus neither minimizes sin nor requires self-cleansing before approach.
Christians must not cast themselves as Jesus in the story. They are the adulterer in the dirt or the hypocrite holding a stone; either way, they need him.

movements.heading: Go tell inexhaustible grace
bullets: The church must tell people that the Lord came not in wrath or judgment but full of grace and truth. Because God came down, believers now invite others to come to him.
Raised hands display how much grace Christ has lavished, yet he remains full and can never run out. Stop running away; run to him and receive peace with God.
Josh closes by marveling that sinners see God’s glory in Jesus and prays for eternal peace through Christ’s blood, singing souls, and victory in his name.

ledger.phrase: “The first 18 verses of John chapter 1”; John’s theology is presented as essential to knowing Jesus.
“The Word was God … The Word became flesh.”
“The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us … [the Son] has made him known.”
“The Lord watches over you … the sun will not harm you by day, nor the moon by night.”
“I will put my dwelling place among you … I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be my people.”
“Is God the God of Jews only? … Yes, of Gentiles too,” since one God justifies both through faith.
The Samaritan woman, worship neither on Gerizim nor in Jerusalem, worship “in the Spirit and in truth,” and Jesus’ “I am he.”
The earthly wilderness tabernacle is a type or shadow of the greater heavenly reality fulfilled in Christ.
The high priest at God’s right hand serves in “the true tabernacle set up by the Lord.”
Christ enters the greater tabernacle and the most holy place once for all “by his own blood,” obtaining eternal redemption.
“We have seen his glory … full of grace and truth”; grace came through Jesus Christ.
God descends on Sinai; boundaries keep the people and priests from coming too near.
Sinai is covered with smoke because the Lord descends in fire, and “the whole mountain trembled violently.”
“Now show me your glory”; “You cannot see my face, for no one may see me and live”; God hides Moses in the rock cleft.
The cloud covers the tent and glory fills it; “Moses could not enter the tent of meeting.”
“To the Israelites the glory of the Lord looked like a consuming fire on top of the mountain.”
“Malachi says God is like a refiner’s fire.”
Jesus teaches in the temple; leaders present a woman caught in adultery and invoke Moses’ command to stone her.
The leaders use the question “as a trap in order to have a basis for accusing him.”
“Let any one of you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.”
“Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you? … Then neither do I condemn you.”
“Go now and leave your life of sin”; grace does not cancel truth.
